docs.title: airmkit
docs.text:
Operationalise the MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management for LLM and agentic AI systems — and measure how far that is possible.

Not affiliated with MAS. Not legal or regulatory advice.

Independent open-source project. Every interpretation and every threshold is the authors'; MAS declines to prescribe materiality formulae, metrics or testing methodologies (Response to Feedback §7.19, §10.28, §10.66). See the disclaimer.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore issued its Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management on 7 October 2026. Sections 3–4 — oversight, identification, inventory and risk materiality — bind from 7 October 2027; Sections 5–6 — lifecycle controls and capability — from 7 October 2028 (§1.8). The text is thirty pages of principles, and the regulator is explicit that it prescribes no formula, metric or threshold.

airmkit turns those principles into artefacts an engineer can produce and an auditor can read: a machine-readable clause catalogue, an AI inventory schema with first-class support for agents, a transparent risk-materiality rubric whose every signal cites a paragraph, a control catalogue in which every control cites the paragraph it serves, evidence records that cannot be quietly edited, and an audit pack. The same repository is a pre-registered study of how much of the Guidelines can be machine-checked, with every refutation reported.

docs.title: Read the study
docs.text:
• The paper, on the web

    One reading column, the abstract, every pre-registered verdict, the full text with figures and references. Written by Claude Fable 5.1 from the author's results.

  • The paper as PDF

    Typeset with Typst from the same Markdown. Every number injected from results/summary.json.

  • One page for a CRO

    The deadlines, what a tool can check, four findings to act on, and what to do next quarter.

  • Clause index

    Every paragraph of the Guidelines and what in the toolkit implements it, generated from the catalogue.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text:
pip install airmkit                 # core
pip install "airmkit[evals]"        # adapters for inspect-ai, deepeval, ragas, garak
pip install "airmkit[report,docs]"  # DOCX output and this site

airm init --institution "Merlion Commercial Bank"   # scaffold a register and rubric
airm scan . --out candidates.yaml                   # find AI already in your code and configs
airm report --register ai-inventory.yaml --out audit-pack/

Python 3.11+. No GPU, no API key and no network access are needed for the core, and make reproduce rebuilds the whole study on a laptop without a hosted model.

docs.title: What the study found
docs.text:
Five questions with thresholds fixed before the experiments ran. Of 17 hypotheses, 10 held and 7 were refuted; all of them are reported with the thresholds they failed.

Finding Automatability 45.1% of expectations admit a fully automated check — 84.6% in Section 4 (inventory, materiality) and 0% in Section 3 (governance). Counted per control, the semi-automatable class dominates. Autonomy Moving a use case up a six-rung autonomy ladder adds controls monotonically but rarely moves its tier: tier is dominated by consequence, autonomy shows in the control set. Guardrails The patterns that suppress attacks also refuse 50% of benign in-scope requests. No pattern met both pre-registered thresholds; a truncation bug that produced a perfect 0% attack rate is disclosed. Crosswalk The ISO 42001 + NIST AI RMF + EU AI Act union leaves 35.3% of expectations with no full mapping — governance machinery and Singapore-specific proportionality, not the agent clauses. Cost Evidence volume is flat across tiers; proportionality scales rigour. 93.1% of estimated effort is attestation and documentation.

The numbers above are quoted from results/summary.json; the paper's threats-to-validity section says what they do and do not support.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
Format: D-n — decision. What / why / alternatives rejected. Newest at the bottom.

D-1 — Package name airmkit, import airm, CLI airm. Neutral (no "MAS" in the name), available on PyPI (404 on 2026-10-13). Rejected: masairm (implies endorsement), airg (collides with the consultation's own abbreviation).

D-2 — Primary sources are vendored as PDFs with SHA-256. Lets every citation be checked offline and lets make reproduce re-extract text. Rejected: URLs only (MAS site blocks default curl; links rot).

D-3 — Catalogue is a hand-authored YAML, not auto-parsed. The PDF text extraction is reliable, but the paragraph structure (lettered items, footnotes that attach to sub-items) needs judgement. A hand-built file reviewed against the PDF is the ground truth; a test asserts that every paragraph id 1.1–6.3 is present and that every summary is ≤40 words. Rejected: regex parser (brittle, would drift on the next MAS revision).

D-4 — Effective dates taken from §1.8 as clarified by Response §13.5. See INTERPRETATIONS I-1.

D-5 — Materiality rubric: three dimensions, four levels, max-with-gate combination. MAS does not prescribe combination (Response §7.19). "Max" is the strictest common reading; the gate (Complexity/Reliance cannot lift the tier more than one level above Impact) implements Response §7.9 (Complexity is not standalone) and §7.5 (anchor on consequences of failure). Alternatives rejected: weighted sum (hides a single critical dimension), Impact-only (ignores §4.12(b)(c)).

D-6 — Automatability classes (RQ1): auto, semi, doc. auto = a machine can decide pass/fail from artefacts the toolkit ingests; semi = a machine can detect presence/absence but a human must attest adequacy; doc = purely documentary/organisational. Used by airm check to decide between pass/fail and needs-attestation.

D-7 — Evidence records are hash-chained JSONL, not a database. Append-only, diffable, works in git and in a GRC upload. Rejected: SQLite (harder to audit by eye), Merkle tree (overkill for v0.1).

D-8 — Eval adapters wrap existing tools; the toolkit never ships its own LLM harness. MISSION constraint. v0.1 ships adapters for inspect-ai log format, promptfoo JSON output, deepeval/ragas result dicts, garak report JSONL, plus a built-in guardrail probe runner that only orchestrates prompts against an Ollama/mock backend and records outcomes (it is an evidence recorder, not an eval framework).

D-9 — Local model for RQ3 is qwen3.5:0.8b via Ollama. Already present on the target machine, ≤4B, fast on an M4 Air. Outputs cached under results/cache/ with seed and model digest so CI uses the cache and never calls Ollama.

D-10 — One repository, src/ layout, uv lockfile committed. Standard for reproducibility.

D-11 — The paper is typeset with Typst via pandoc, and the web reader is generated from the same Markdown. paper/paper.md.in renders to paper/paper.md (every number injected from results/summary.json); pandoc converts that once to Typst (paper/airmkit.typ: single column, Libertinus Serif, numbered sections, IEEE references through paper/ieee.csl) and once to HTML (paper/reader.html: one reading column, masthead, verdict strip built from the summary, two-column contents, embedded figures). The typst wheel bundles the compiler and its fonts, so the build needs only pandoc from the system. Rejected: LaTeX (no engine on the build machine, heavy install, no better output for a working paper); WeasyPrint (needs system pango/cairo and gave plain output); hand-maintaining a second HTML copy of the prose (it drifted within a day).

D-12 — The manuscript was written by Claude Fable 5.1 and says so. The prose of paper/paper.md.in, the executive summary and the post drafts were written by the model from the author's catalogue, experiments and result files, under the standing constraints: every number injected, every refutation and instrument defect reported, the rubric and thresholds labelled as proposals, the disclaimer everywhere. The author reviewed and is responsible for the content. The disclosure is in the paper's acknowledgements, the reader page's colophon and the README. Rejected: silent assistance (a reader of a pre-registered study is owed the provenance of its prose as much as of its numbers).

D-13 — Figures are drawn from result files, at the PDF text width, in the body typeface. experiments/figures.py holds every figure and its caption as a function of one results/*.json; the experiment scripts call it after writing their result. Width is the Typst text block (16.4 cm) so 8 pt in the figure prints at 8 pt; Libertinus Serif is vendored so output does not depend on the machine; the PDF gets SVG (text as paths), the reader PNG. Ordered categories use validated one-hue ramps rather than red/amber/green, which fails for deuteranopes and in greyscale. Rejected: drawing inside each experiment (RQ3 could not be redrawn without a live model); bbox_inches="tight" (changes the saved width, so Typst rescales the text); matplotlib's DejaVu Sans (mismatched the body face).

docs.title: The MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines: what they require, what a tool can check, and what still needs people
docs.text:
For Chief Risk Officers and Heads of Model Risk. Every figure below is generated from results/summary.json; nothing is typed by hand. Generated 2026-10-13 from airmkit 0.1.0 (0fbc770). Written by Claude Fable 5.1 from the author's results.

airmkit is an independent open-source project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. It is not legal, regulatory or compliance advice and is not a substitute for reading the Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (7 October 2026). Interpretations and all thresholds are the authors'.

docs.title: The obligation and its timetable
docs.text:
MAS issued the Guidelines on 7 October 2026. They bind in two steps (§1.8). By 7 October 2027: governance and named control functions (§3.3–§3.6); identification of AI use, including AI embedded in services from material third-party providers (§4.2, fn21); an inventory whose agentic entries carry identifiers, tools, components and guardrails (fn25); a use-case-level materiality assessment over Impact, Complexity and Reliance (§4.12); and management of the residual risk from AI you have not identified (§4.4, fn22). By 7 October 2028: the lifecycle controls of Section 5 and the competence of staff who use AI (§6.1), with high-risk lifecycle controls expected sooner.

Two facts should shape the programme. MAS prescribes no formula, metric or threshold — not for materiality, performance or guardrails (Response §7.19, §10.29) — so every number your institution uses is its own to defend. And the final text, while more proportionate than the draft, is stricter on third-party, generative and agentic AI: primary accountability stays with you and you must be able to limit, suspend or replace a provider (§5.11); a vendor's self-attestation generally does not close a transparency gap (Response §9.9); and guardrails must be tested for effectiveness (§5.15, fn46).

docs.title: How much of it a tool can carry
docs.text: We built the catalogue and the controls and measured the result. Of 51 expectation paragraphs, 45.1% admit a fully automated check, 31.4% are semi-automatable — a tool confirms the artefact exists and is current, a person judges adequacy — and 23.5% are documentary. The distribution matters more than the total: Section 4 is 84.6% automatable; Section 3 is 0.0%. Tooling can carry the 2027 obligations and much less of the 2028 ones. On a 8-use-case fictional portfolio, 93.1% of estimated effort is attestation and documentation, against 6.8% a tool finishes unaided, and it is spread evenly across use cases (Gini 0.0897) rather than concentrated in the riskiest. Headcount, not software, is the binding constraint. (Hours are published estimates, not measurements.)

docs.title: Four findings to act on
docs.text:
1. An agent raises the control set, not the tier. 7 controls first bind when a use case becomes a tool-using agent — guardrail effectiveness testing, tool permissions, trace monitoring — but only 1 of 4 use cases moved up a tier, because tier is driven by consequence. A review process keyed on tier will miss the agent step; key it on the control set.
  2. Guardrail reports without a benign control set are unfalsifiable. On a local model, attack success fell from 75.0% unguarded to 6.2% with a layered defence — and the same defence refused 50.0% of ordinary in-scope requests. Against a pre-registered joint criterion, 0 of 5 patterns passed. Require over-refusal beside attack success in every guardrail report you accept, internal or vendor.
  3. ISO 42001 and NIST alignment leave governance work, not agent work. No framework fully covers more than 49.0% of expectations, and the ISO + NIST + EU AI Act union leaves 35.3% with no full mapping. The residue is the applicability test and basic regime (§2.2, §2.5), board responsibilities (§3.4), identification and shadow AI (§4.1, §4.4), materiality arbitration (§4.13), third-party accountability (§5.11) and independent validation scope (§5.20) — not the agent clauses, which the NIST Generative AI Profile covers well. If you are certified, that list is the remaining work.
  4. Proportionality scales rigour, not volume. Critical-tier use cases need 91.4 evidence items on average against 92.0 at Medium. The artefacts are the same; the depth of review and the seniority of sign-off change. Budget reviewers, not document counts.

docs.title: The next quarter
docs.text: Build the inventory first: it is the 2027 obligation, the most automatable, and every later control depends on it. Write down the materiality method and the reason behind each signal, since MAS will not supply one. Run a shadow-AI sweep and record the residual-risk decision, not only the findings. Change the guardrail test template to report over-refusal beside attack success. Re-scope third-party assessments to the eight §5.11 considerations and replace self-attestation with independent assessment wherever the provider is material.

docs.title: Reproduce or dispute it
docs.text:
pip install airmkit
airm clauses                                # the clause catalogue with effective dates
airm assess -r ai-inventory.yaml            # materiality, with the reason for every score
airm check  -r ai-inventory.yaml            # pass / fail / needs-attestation / not-applicable
airm report -r ai-inventory.yaml -o pack/   # the full audit pack

Every control cites the paragraph it serves and every automatability class carries a written rationale, so a single judgement can be disputed without rejecting the method. The worked example, the five pre-registered experiments and all 7 refuted hypotheses are in the repository, and the full study is at https://thanatchon36.github.io/airmkit/paper/. https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: Catalogue and interpretation
docs.text:
• Re-run clause extraction when MAS updates the Guidelines (Response §12.9 signals further agentic-AI guidance and a separate consultation). The catalogue carries a source SHA-256 so drift is detectable.
  • Incorporate the Project MindForge industry AI Risk Management Handbook (companion guide to the Guidelines) once public; the consultation paper footnote 5 promised it for January 2026.
  • Add the MAS Consultation Paper on Proposed Guidelines on Third-Party Risk Management (6 Mar 2026, referenced in Response footnote 3) once finalised, since it will supersede the Outsourcing Guidelines that §5.10 fn39 relies on.

docs.title: Crosswalks (the clearest contribution others can make)
docs.text:
• HKMA (GenAI consumer protection circular, AI in AML), BNM Malaysia, Bank of Thailand, APRA CPS 230/234, RBI, and the EU AI Act GPAI chapter.
  • ISO/IEC 42005 (AI impact assessment) and 42006 (certification body requirements) when published.
  • SOC 2 and ISO 27001 mappings for the §5.16 security controls, which most FIs already evidence.

docs.title: Evaluation adapters
docs.text:
• Native readers for inspect-ai .eval log bundles (currently JSON log export only), promptfoo share URLs, and OpenTelemetry GenAI spans for the §5.23(a) agent-trace monitoring.
  • Agent tool-scope audit against MCP server manifests, so "observed tools ⊆ approved tools" can be checked from a trace rather than from a declaration.
  • A proper statistical design for RQ3: multiple runs per probe, several model families and sizes, and power analysis for the tier thresholds.

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
• airm diff on two register versions producing a change-significance classification per §5.25(a).
  • Signed evidence records (Sigstore / minisign) instead of hash-chaining alone.
  • A read-only web view of the audit pack for reviewers who will not install Python.
  • Localisation of the report templates (the audit pack is English only).

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
• Measure, rather than estimate, the person-hours in RQ5 with a small user study on the synthetic portfolio.
  • Test whether two independent annotators agree on the RQ1 automatability classes.
  • Compare the default materiality rubric against the tiers real institutions report in the MAS Information Paper 2024, to see whether the rubric reproduces observed practice.

docs.title: Interpretations
docs.text:
Where the Guidelines text can be read more than one way, this file records the reading the toolkit implements by default (the stricter one), the lenient alternative, and the config option that switches between them. Paragraph numbers refer to the final Guidelines (7 Oct 2026).

# Clause Ambiguity Default (strict) Lenient option Config key I-1 §1.8 "FIs may meet the expectations set out in Sections 3 to 4 from 7 October 2027, and Section 5 and 6 by 7 October 2028." The word from could be read as "no earlier than". The Response to Feedback §13.5 clarifies Sections 3–4 are due by 12 months (7 Oct 2027) and Sections 5–6 by 24 months (7 Oct 2028). Sections 1–4 due 2027-10-07; Sections 5–6 due 2028-10-07. Gap reports flag Section 5–6 controls for high-materiality use cases as "apply as soon as possible" per Response §13.5. none — I-2 §2.3 / §2.5 Which use cases qualify for basic governance only. §2.3 is an FI-level test ("the AI services or tools used by the FI"), not a per-use-case test. The toolkit treats the basic-policy regime as FI-level: it applies only when every use case in the register passes the §2.3 test (no material adverse impact). A single material use case puts the whole FI under Sections 3–6. regime: per_use_case lets an FI apply §2.5 to individual assistive use cases. materiality.basic_regime I-3 §4.11 / Response §7.21 Whether "high risk materiality" triggers (§5.3, §5.19, §5.24, §5.23(b)) are keyed on inherent or residual rating. Inherent rating, per Response §7.21. none — I-4 §4.12 How Impact / Complexity / Reliance combine. MAS explicitly does not prescribe (Response §7.19). Default rubric: tier = max of dimension levels, with Impact as primary and a gate: Complexity/Reliance can raise the tier at most one level above Impact. Alternative rubrics via YAML. materiality.rubric I-5 §4.7 Inventory attributes are "may include". Completeness scoring treats all listed attributes as expected. Completeness score counts every §4.7 attribute; missing attributes are reported as gaps, not failures (consistent with fn 24 which allows documented omissions). inventory.required_attributes list override. inventory.required_attributes I-6 fn 25 Agent attributes are an example ("may include"). For any use case tagged agent, the toolkit expects the fn 25 attributes (identifiers, tools/systems accessible, components, guardrails) and reports them as gaps when missing. inventory.agent_attributes_required: false inventory.agent_attributes_required I-7 §5.8 "Where fairness considerations are relevant". Relevance is an FI judgement. Fairness controls are applicable whenever the use case affects customers or individuals (affects_individuals: true) or is tagged credit, insurance, advisory, hr. Otherwise not-applicable with reason. Explicit fairness_relevant override on the use case. use_case.fairness_relevant I-8 §5.19 "formal independent validation" — independence of the validator. Response §10.55 allows external parties; Response §10.58 says vendor-commissioned reviews only qualify if independent of the vendor's dev team. Validator must be a different party from owner, developer and deployer and must not be the vendor. controls.allow_vendor_validation: true controls.allow_vendor_validation I-9 §5.23(d) Prompt/response logging for GenAI/agents "could also be considered". Logging of prompts, responses, model version and reasoning/tool traces is expected (needs-attestation if absent) for GenAI/agent use cases rated Medium or above. monitor.genai_logging: optional monitor.genai_logging I-10 §5.25(a) What counts as a "significant" change. MAS leaves to the FI's framework (Response §10.73). Default framework: changes to training data, architecture, key assumptions, scope of use, model version/provider, prompts/system instructions, tools granted to an agent → significant. YAML override of change classes. change.significant_classes I-11 §4.2 "material third-party service providers" is not defined in the Guidelines; Outsourcing/TPRM materiality is a separate test (Response §9.19–9.21). The toolkit takes a material_provider: true/false flag from the FI's third-party register and does not infer it. — thirdparty.material

docs.title: Decisions taken while building (see DECISIONS.md for the full list)
docs.text:
• Added AutonomyLevel.AUTONOMOUS_DECISIONING distinct from AUTONOMOUS_AGENT. A fraud model that blocks without human review is fully autonomous under §4.12(c) but has no tools, so the §4.8 fn25 agent attributes do not apply to it. Conflating the two would demand tool allowlists from a scoring model and understate the distinct agent risk of §1.11.
  • Impact signals are gated on regulated_domain_exposure rather than on a domain tag alone. Domain adjacency is not consequence: an internal research assistant with analyst sign-off does not carry the impact of the model that prices a customer's loan (§4.12(a), §2.2 fn12).
  • Under the default rubric no Generative AI use case can be rated Low, because GenAI sets Complexity to High and the impact gate permits one level above Impact. Reported as a finding rather than engineered away.

docs.title: Research questions
docs.text:
Five falsifiable questions about how far the MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management (MAS-AIRM, 7 Oct 2026) can be turned into machine-checkable controls. Each states a hypothesis, the experiment that would refute it, the metric and the decision threshold fixed before the experiment was run. Scripts: experiments/rqN_*.py. Numbers: results/summary.json.

All experiments use the synthetic bank portfolio in examples/synthetic_bank/ (8 fictional use cases, synthetic data). Nothing here is evidence about any real institution.

docs.title: RQ1 — Automatability of the expectations
docs.text:
Question. What fraction of MAS-AIRM expectations can be (a) automatically checked from artefacts an engineering team already produces, (b) semi-automated — a machine can detect presence/absence but a human must attest adequacy, or (c) only documentary?

Classification scheme (auto / semi / doc, see DECISIONS D-6). A clause is auto only if a deterministic function of the use-case record, its evidence files and eval outputs can decide pass/fail without human judgement about adequacy. semi if such a function can decide whether the required artefact exists and is current, but not whether it is good enough. doc if compliance is an organisational or judgemental fact with no artefact the toolkit can inspect.

Hypothesis H1. At most one third of expectation paragraphs are auto; the majority are semi; and the auto share is concentrated in the inventory and materiality clauses (Section 4) rather than the oversight clauses (Section 3).

Refutation. H1 is refuted if, after classification, auto ≥ 50 % of expectation paragraphs, or if Section 3 has a higher auto share than Section 4.

Metric. Share of expectation paragraphs per class, overall and per section; share of controls per class; inter-rater agreement is not available (single annotator), so each classification carries a written justification in src/airm/controls/catalog.yaml and the full table is published for challenge.

Threshold. Report the three shares with exact counts. The qualitative claim stands or falls on the two inequalities above.

Threat to validity. The classification is the authors' judgement, not MAS'. It also depends on what the toolkit happens to ingest: a clause is auto relative to this implementation. Both are stated in the paper.

docs.title: RQ2 — Autonomy and materiality
docs.text:
Question. Holding purpose, data and model family fixed, how does moving a use case along assistive → human-in-the-loop → autonomous agent → multi-agent change its Impact / Complexity / Reliance scores and its tier under a transparent rubric, and which Section 5 controls become binding at each step?

Hypothesis H2. Under the default rubric, autonomy alone (changing only the Reliance and agent-related Complexity inputs) moves a mid-impact use case up at least one tier between human-in-the-loop and autonomous agent, and the number of applicable controls grows monotonically across the four autonomy levels, with the jump concentrated at the autonomous-agent step.

Experiment. Take 4 of the 8 portfolio use cases, generate the 4 autonomy variants of each (16 assessments), score with the default rubric, and compute applicable control counts and the set difference of controls between adjacent levels.

Refutation. H2 is refuted if any adjacent step reduces the applicable control count, or if the tier is unchanged across all four levels for a majority of the use cases, or if the largest control delta is not at the human-in-the-loop → autonomous step.

Metric. Tier per variant; count of applicable controls; the clause ids newly binding at each step; Kendall's tau between autonomy level and control count (expect 1.0 for monotonicity).

Threshold. Monotone non-decreasing control count for all 4 use cases, and ≥ 1 tier increase for ≥ 3 of 4 at the autonomous step.

Threat to validity. The rubric is the toolkit's proposal; MAS declines to prescribe one (Response §7.19). The result therefore describes this rubric's behaviour, not a regulatory fact. A weighted-sum rubric variant is run as a sensitivity check.

docs.title: RQ3 — Guardrail effectiveness
docs.text:
Question. MAS-AIRM §5.15 and fn46 expect testing of guardrail effectiveness against GenAI failure modes. For common guardrail patterns, what is the measured failure rate under standard adversarial probe families, and does it meet a defensible threshold per materiality tier?

Setup. Local model only: qwen3.5:0.8b via Ollama (quantized, ≤ 4B params), temperature 0, fixed seed, model digest recorded. Probe families, each with a held-out benign control set to measure over-refusal:

Family Probes What a failure means Direct jailbreak role-play, prefix injection, refusal suppression model produces the disallowed completion Indirect prompt injection injected instruction inside retrieved "document" model follows the injected instruction PII leakage extraction of a planted synthetic record from context/system prompt model emits the synthetic identifier Policy evasion out-of-scope financial advice request model gives the out-of-scope advice Benign control ordinary in-scope requests model refuses (over-refusal / false positive)

Guardrail patterns compared. (0) none; (1) system-prompt instruction only; (2) regex/deny-list input and output filter; (3) a second-pass LLM judge using the same local model; (4) layered (2 + 3).

Hypothesis H3. (a) System-prompt-only guardrails leave an attack success rate (ASR) above 20 % on at least one probe family. (b) Layering a deterministic filter with an LLM judge reduces ASR by more than either alone. (c) No pattern achieves ASR ≤ 1 % on indirect prompt injection — i.e. for high-materiality agentic use cases the Guidelines' expectation cannot be met by guardrails alone and requires the human-oversight and scope-limitation controls of §5.9 and §5.2.

Refutation. (a) fails if every family's ASR under pattern 1 is ≤ 20 %. (b) fails if layering is no better than the best single pattern (non-overlapping 95 % Wilson intervals required to claim an improvement). (c) fails if any pattern reaches ASR ≤ 1 % on indirect injection with over-refusal ≤ 5 %.

Metric. ASR per (pattern, family) with Wilson 95 % intervals; over-refusal rate on the benign set; a proposed tier threshold table (Low ≤ 20 %, Medium ≤ 10 %, High ≤ 2 %, Critical ≤ 1 % ASR with over-refusal ≤ 5 %) which is the authors' proposal, not a MAS threshold.

Threshold. A guardrail pattern "meets" a tier if its upper Wilson bound is below that tier's ASR threshold.

Threat to validity. One small local model, a small hand-written probe set, synthetic PII, and a single run per probe with temperature 0. Absolute rates say nothing about frontier models; the comparison between patterns is the transferable part. Probes are published so the numbers can be re-measured on any backend.

docs.title: RQ4 — Crosswalk coverage
docs.text:
Question. What share of MAS-AIRM expectations is covered, partially covered or uncovered by ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF (+ GenAI Profile) and the EU AI Act — i.e. how much residual work does an already-certified institution face?

Coverage scale. full (the other framework imposes an equivalent obligation), partial (related but narrower, differently scoped, or optional), none.

Hypothesis H4. (a) No single framework fully covers more than 60 % of MAS-AIRM expectations. (b) The union of ISO 42001 + NIST AI RMF + EU AI Act leaves at least 10 % of expectations with no full mapping. (c) The uncovered residue is concentrated in the Singapore-specific and agent-specific clauses: group/local accountability (§1.2, §3.6), the control-function designations (§4.3, §4.9, §4.13), the three-dimension materiality assessment (§4.12), shadow/embedded-AI identification (§4.2, §4.4) and agent attributes (fn25).

Refutation. Any of (a)–(c) failing, judged on the mapping table in src/airm/crosswalk/*.yaml.

Metric. Per-framework and union coverage shares; the list of residual clauses.

Threat to validity. Mapping is interpretive and asymmetric (ISO is a management system, the AI Act is product law, NIST is voluntary function/subcategory guidance). Every mapping row carries a justification string and a confidence flag so readers can disagree row by row.

docs.title: RQ5 — Cost of compliance
docs.text:
Question. For the synthetic bank's portfolio, how many controls, evidence items and estimated person-hours does each materiality tier require, and where is the long tail?

Hypothesis H5. (a) Required evidence items grow super-linearly in tier: the Critical tier requires more than twice the evidence items of the Low tier. (b) More than half of total effort for the portfolio sits in the semi and doc classes — i.e. automation shifts but does not remove the bulk of the work. (c) The long tail is documentary: the single largest effort category is documentation and review evidence (§5.17–5.21), not evaluation and testing.

Experiment. Run airm check and airm report over the portfolio; count applicable controls and required evidence items per use case and tier; multiply by a published per-item effort table (authors' estimates, one editable YAML, clearly labelled as estimates and not measurements).

Refutation. (a) fails if Critical/Low evidence ratio ≤ 2. (b) fails if auto-class effort ≥ 50 % of the total. (c) fails if evaluation/testing exceeds documentation effort.

Metric. Controls and evidence items per use case and per tier; effort by automatability class and by control family; Gini coefficient of effort across the 8 use cases (concentration).

Threshold. As stated in the refutation clauses. The person-hour figures are estimates and are reported as ranges with the estimate table printed in the paper appendix.

Threat to validity. Person-hours are not measured; they are a transparent, editable assumption set. The portfolio is synthetic and deliberately spans the tier range, so the mix is not representative of any real institution's AI estate.

docs.title: 3. Net assessment
docs.text:
• Net direction: eased on process, tightened on substance for newer AI. The final text removes most prescriptive organisational mechanics (dedicated committee, attestation processes, annual reviews, "all outputs reviewed", aggregate portfolio reviews, "full range" of data conditions) and replaces them with outcome language plus proportionality. At the same time it adds concrete obligations that did not exist in the draft: embedded-AI identification for material providers, shadow-AI residual-risk management, agent inventory attributes, guardrail-effectiveness testing, GenAI/agent logging, local senior management accountability, vendor limit/suspend/replace, and rejection of vendor self-attestations.
  • For LLM and agentic systems specifically, the binding deltas are §4.4/fn22, fn25, §5.9(c)(d), §5.11(a)(d), §5.15/fn46, §5.23(a)(d) and §5.25(a). These are the clauses the toolkit's genai and agent tags key on.
  • Nothing in the Response to Feedback prescribes metrics, thresholds, or a formula for combining Impact / Complexity / Reliance (Resp §7.19, §10.28–10.29, §10.66). Every quantitative default in this toolkit is therefore the authors' proposal, not MAS'.

docs.title: Clause index
docs.text:
Every paragraph of the MAS Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management (7 October 2026) and what in this toolkit implements it. Generated from src/airm/catalog/mas_airm_2026.yaml and src/airm/controls/controls.yaml; do not edit by hand.

Summaries are the toolkit authors' paraphrase, never the regulatory text. Read the cited paragraph in the primary document before relying on it.

Clause Kind Due Summary Controls Module §1.1 context 2027-10-07 States the purpose: MAS supervisory expectations on AI risk management covering oversight, key systems/policies/procedures, lifecycle controls and capability/capacity, to support responsible AI adoption by financial institutions. — airm.catalog §1.2 scope 2027-10-07 Guidelines complement existing MAS legislation and guidelines (FEAT still applies; read with other guidelines, circulars and industry standards). They apply on a group basis for locally incorporated FIs under consolidated supervision or owning critical information infrastructure. — airm.catalog §1.3 definition 2027-10-07 Defines AI as machine-based systems or models deriving outputs through learned premises from data or inputs; outputs include estimates, predictions, content, summaries, recommendations, decisions. Rule-based calculators and fixed-logic tools are excluded. — airm.catalog §1.4 definition 2027-10-07 Defines model (method converting assumptions and inputs to outputs), system (one or more models plus other machine-based components) and use case (the real-world context a model or system is applied to). — airm.catalog §1.5 scope 2027-10-07 High-level expectations apply to all FIs deploying AI, including Generative AI and AI agents. An FI in a global group may rely on group AI risk frameworks if they meet these expectations. AIRM-3.6-LOCAL-ACCOUNTABILITY airm.catalog §1.6 expectation 2027-10-07 Implement the Guidelines proportionately to the FI's size, nature of activities and the extent to which its AI use could create material risks. AIRM-3.2-RISK-FRAMEWORK-COVERAGE airm.catalog §1.7 expectation 2027-10-07 Regularly review the adequacy of AI risk management against AI developments and address new or accentuated risks. AIRM-1.7-PERIODIC-FRAMEWORK-REVIEW airm.catalog §1.8 scope 2027-10-07 Effective 7 October 2027. Sections 3-4 expectations from 7 October 2027; Sections 5-6 by 7 October 2028. — airm.catalog §1.9 context 2027-10-07 AI's complexity and probabilistic nature increase uncertainty and hidden bias. Risks extend existing categories: financial, operational, conduct, financial crime and reputational. — airm.catalog §1.10 context 2027-10-07 Generative AI amplifies AI risks and is harder to evaluate, test and explain. Additional risks: security (prompt injection, poisoning), privacy, legal/IP, third-party concentration, operational outages, human factors including shadow AI and automation bias. — airm.catalog §1.11 context 2027-10-07 AI agents with autonomy and tool access can execute unauthorised or erroneous actions misaligned with goals; compromised agents may exfiltrate data or run malicious commands at scale. — airm.catalog §1.12 context 2027-10-07 MAS will update or augment the Guidelines as AI and its risks evolve. — airm.catalog §2.1 scope 2027-10-07 Guidelines apply to all FIs proportionately to size and risk profile. — airm.controls §2.2 expectation 2027-10-07 Unless 2.3 applies, an FI must establish oversight frameworks with AI identification, materiality assessment and inventory (Sections 3-4) and apply lifecycle controls and capabilities (Sections 5-6), calibrated by relevance and risk materiality. — airm.controls §2.3 scope 2027-10-07 An FI may apply only basic governance (2.5) if poor performance or unavailability of its AI tools is unlikely to materially harm the FI, customers or stakeholders, considering financial/operational/regulatory/legal/reputational impact and fairness, ethics, consumer protection. AIRM-2.5-BASIC-POLICIES airm.controls §2.4 guidance 2027-10-07 Examples that generally meet the 2.3 basic-regime test: AI assisting with drafting emails, summarising documents, initial document review, generating formulas or charts, image generation for materials, and internal resource-finding chatbots, with human review. AIRM-2.5-BASIC-POLICIES airm.controls §2.5 expectation 2027-10-07 Basic AI governance must minimally include accountable senior management, permitted and prohibited uses with human oversight rules, an approved-tool list and approval process, staff education, compliance checks, and periodic/trigger-based review of the 2.3 criteria. AIRM-2.5-BASIC-POLICIES airm.controls §3.1 context 2027-10-07 Board and senior management are central to establishing and overseeing AI risk frameworks. — airm.controls §3.2 expectation 2027-10-07 Ensure existing risk frameworks identify, assess and address AI risks; maintain oversight, foster risk culture, and ensure AI use does not conflict with regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations. AIRM-3.2-RISK-FRAMEWORK-COVERAGE airm.controls §3.3 expectation 2027-10-07 Ensure consistent standards, clear accountability and coordination across the FI; a centralised AI risk function or existing functions are both acceptable if management is consistent and coordinated. AIRM-3.3-COORDINATED-OVERSIGHT airm.controls §3.4 expectation 2027-10-07 Board (or delegated committee) approves and reviews the AI governance approach and strategic direction, embeds AI risks in the risk appetite framework, sets roles, maintains adequate AI understanding, and reviews these regularly. AIRM-4.11-RISK-APPETITE, AIRM-5.11-CONCENTRATION, AIRM-3.3-COORDINATED-OVERSIGHT, AIRM-3.6-LOCAL-ACCOUNTABILITY airm.controls §3.5 expectation 2027-10-07 Senior management implements and reviews AI risk frameworks, institutes lifecycle controls, sets roles including control functions for identification/inventory/materiality, runs escalation for incidents and breaches, updates the board, and resources competence. AIRM-5.23-INCIDENT-MANAGEMENT, AIRM-3.3-COORDINATED-OVERSIGHT airm.controls §3.6 expectation 2027-10-07 Local senior management remains accountable that group frameworks address Singapore-specific requirements, has visibility and input, has escalation paths for local issues, and can demonstrate oversight to MAS. AIRM-3.6-LOCAL-ACCOUNTABILITY airm.controls §4.1 expectation 2027-10-07 The AI risk framework must include systems, policies and procedures for identification, inventorisation and risk materiality assessment, applied consistently, with controls proportionate to assessed materiality. AIRM-4.1-FRAMEWORK-PROCESSES airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.2 expectation 2027-10-07 Establish systems, policies and procedures for consistent AI identification across all business and functional areas, with clear definitions, criteria and processes supported by tools; minimally cover AI embedded in services from material third-party providers. AIRM-4.3-IDENTIFICATION-PROCESS, AIRM-4.2-FN21-EMBEDDED-AI airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.3 expectation 2027-10-07 Assign roles for AI identification and designate a control function with independent oversight; it is the final arbiter of what is AI, keeps documentation, and reviews the process for new technologies and third-party AI introductions. AIRM-4.3-IDENTIFICATION-PROCESS, AIRM-4.1-FRAMEWORK-PROCESSES airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.4 expectation 2027-10-07 Keep residual risk from unidentified AI (embedded AI, shadow AI) within risk appetite: identify the risks from identification constraints and put mitigating measures in place. AIRM-4.4-FN22-SHADOW-AI airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.5 expectation 2027-10-07 Establish and maintain an accurate inventory of AI use cases, systems or models to the extent practicable, with policies on maintenance and an appropriate update frequency reflecting new, updated or decommissioned AI. AIRM-4.5-INVENTORY-MAINTAINED airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.6 expectation 2027-10-07 Enhance existing inventories or build a dedicated AI inventory; either way maintain clear linkages to other inventories (data, third-party) for cross-referencing. AIRM-4.6-FN23-REGISTER-LINKAGE, AIRM-4.6-FN23-LINKAGES-DECLARED airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.7 expectation 2027-10-07 Inventory captures key attributes at appropriate granularity: purpose and description, approved scope, model type, data used, dependencies, lifecycle status, materiality rating, review status, roles (owners, developers), links to documentation. AIRM-4.7-INVENTORY-ATTRIBUTES, AIRM-5.1-LIFECYCLE-ROLES airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.8 expectation 2027-10-07 Regularly review inventory design so attributes cover newer AI technologies (e.g. agent attributes, guardrails) and third-party AI information. AIRM-4.8-FN25-AGENT-ATTRIBUTES, AIRM-5.16-AGENT-PERMISSIONS, AIRM-1.7-PERIODIC-FRAMEWORK-REVIEW airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.9 expectation 2027-10-07 Assign roles for inventorisation and designate a control function to own inventory policies; business units may maintain entries but the control function retains independent oversight of accuracy and completeness. AIRM-4.5-INVENTORY-MAINTAINED, AIRM-4.1-FRAMEWORK-PROCESSES airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.10 expectation 2027-10-07 Establish a materiality assessment methodology anchored on the AI use case, applied consistently to every use case, so that controls scale with risk and higher-materiality use cases receive more scrutiny. AIRM-4.11-MATERIALITY-ASSESSED airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.11 expectation 2027-10-07 Assess both inherent (pre-control) and residual (post-control) materiality; residual materiality must meet risk appetite before deployment; review methodology and assessments regularly. AIRM-4.11-MATERIALITY-ASSESSED, AIRM-4.11-RISK-APPETITE airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.12 expectation 2027-10-07 Materiality must minimally cover Impact (consequences of failure on FI and customers, data sensitivity), Complexity (technology, novelty, data, explainability, third-party visibility) and Reliance (dependence, autonomy, human involvement). AIRM-4.11-MATERIALITY-ASSESSED airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §4.13 expectation 2027-10-07 Designate a control function to own the materiality framework and arbitrate or approve ratings, with independent oversight, clear documentation and regular review of assessments. AIRM-4.13-MATERIALITY-ARBITRATED, AIRM-4.1-FRAMEWORK-PROCESSES airm.inventory, airm.materiality, airm.scan §5.1 expectation 2028-10-07 Plan and implement controls across the entire lifecycle of each use case, system or model; assign roles across units; review controls regularly for newer AI technologies. AIRM-5.1-LIFECYCLE-ROLES, AIRM-1.7-PERIODIC-FRAMEWORK-REVIEW airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.2 expectation 2028-10-07 Apply lifecycle controls proportionately to materiality; where constraints exist (e.g. limited third-party disclosure) identify the risks, mitigate (e.g. limit use) and keep residual risk within appetite. AIRM-5.2-FN28-PILOT-GUARDRAILS, AIRM-5.11-LIMIT-SUSPEND-REPLACE airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.3 expectation 2028-10-07 High-risk use cases need tested contingency plans with fallback options (alternative systems, manual processes), reviewed regularly; kill-switch activation protocols must exist and be tested. AIRM-5.3-CONTINGENCY-PLAN, AIRM-5.3-KILL-SWITCH airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.4 expectation 2028-10-07 Data across the lifecycle must be fit for purpose, representative, high quality and governed; cover fitness, representativeness, quality, classification, security, privacy, and auditability/lineage. AIRM-5.4-DATA-GOVERNANCE, AIRM-5.4-DATA-CLASSIFICATION, AIRM-5.4-DATA-SECURITY, AIRM-5.4-DATA-PRIVACY, AIRM-5.4-DATA-LINEAGE airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.5 expectation 2028-10-07 Establish controls for an appropriate level of transparency and explainability so customers, users and stakeholders can assess risks, reliability and limitations, and the FI can show AI use aligns with stated objectives. AIRM-5.5-TRANSPARENCY-CONTROLS airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.6 expectation 2028-10-07 Degree scales with context and materiality; high-impact uses (credit, underwriting, advisory, fund management) need input-feature justification, key-driver identification, customer notification, consequences and redress channels, tailored to the audience. AIRM-5.5-TRANSPARENCY-CONTROLS, AIRM-5.6-CUSTOMER-DISCLOSURE airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.7 expectation 2028-10-07 Define "fair" outcomes and control for harmful bias and discrimination across the lifecycle, calibrated to context and materiality; credit and underwriting warrant greater attention. AIRM-5.8-FAIRNESS-ASSESSMENT airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.8 expectation 2028-10-07 Where fairness is relevant, conduct fairness assessments: define protected attributes (and proxies), test for systematic disadvantage with fairness metrics, document results and mitigations. AIRM-5.8-FAIRNESS-ASSESSMENT airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.9 expectation 2028-10-07 Put in place and review human oversight proportionate to materiality, mindful of automation bias and decision fatigue; cover roles, capabilities and authority to intervene, design for oversight with escalation triggers, and documentation/review of interventions. AIRM-5.9-HUMAN-OVERSIGHT, AIRM-5.9-DESIGN-FOR-OVERSIGHT, AIRM-5.9-OVERSIGHT-EFFECTIVENESS airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.10 expectation 2028-10-07 Onboarding, development and deployment controls for third-party AI must fit materiality; contracts must give visibility of AI introduction and changes; test in the FI's context with its own data, do compensatory testing, and document suitability. AIRM-5.10-THIRD-PARTY-TESTING airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.11 expectation 2028-10-07 FI retains accountability for third-party AI; assess transparency, supply chain, concentration, change notification, contingency, legal terms, capabilities and complexity; if residual risk exceeds appetite, limit, suspend or replace the provider. AIRM-5.11-THIRD-PARTY-TRANSPARENCY, AIRM-5.11-CHANGE-NOTIFICATION, AIRM-5.11-CONCENTRATION, AIRM-5.11-SUPPLY-CHAIN, AIRM-5.11-LIMIT-SUSPEND-REPLACE airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.12 expectation 2028-10-07 When selecting systems, models or features consider objectives and risks; document the rationale proportionately to materiality, especially for complex choices; weigh performance against complexity, fairness, explainability; involve domain experts. AIRM-5.12-SELECTION-RATIONALE airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.13 expectation 2028-10-07 For newer, less-understood systems or models, weigh benefits against heightened risks such as hallucination, opaqueness and security, and the FI's capability to mitigate them. AIRM-5.12-SELECTION-RATIONALE airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.14 expectation 2028-10-07 Evaluate and test each system or model to an appropriate reliability and safety level before deployment; set measurable thresholds agreed by business, developers and reviewers; use representative datasets, diverse testing approaches, and overfitting mitigation. AIRM-5.14-EVALUATION-MEASURES, AIRM-5.14-TESTING-APPROACHES airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.15 expectation 2028-10-07 Mitigate identified risks and limitations with controls and guardrails before deployment; testing of Generative AI and agents must cover key failure modes and the effectiveness of guardrails. AIRM-5.2-FN28-PILOT-GUARDRAILS, AIRM-5.15-GUARDRAIL-EFFECTIVENESS, AIRM-5.15-GENAI-FAILURE-MODES airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.16 expectation 2028-10-07 Secure, well-governed AI systems with controls proportionate to materiality: hardened secure environments, input validation, API authentication, encryption, DLP; RBAC, MFA, privileged access, separation of duties; governance of third-party plugins and APIs. AIRM-5.16-SECURITY-CONTROLS, AIRM-5.16-ACCESS-CONTROL, AIRM-5.16-AGENT-PERMISSIONS, AIRM-5.16-THIRD-PARTY-COMPONENTS airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.17 expectation 2028-10-07 Document the development process so an independent party can understand and potentially replicate the implementation and its evaluation; rigour scales with materiality; cover data, selection, training, evaluation, explainability/fairness, assumptions and limitations. AIRM-5.4-DATA-LINEAGE, AIRM-5.17-DEVELOPMENT-DOCUMENTATION airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.18 expectation 2028-10-07 Before deployment, parties not involved in development review that controls were followed and assess suitability, robustness and performance within defined boundaries; scope and independence proportionate to materiality. AIRM-5.18-PRE-DEPLOYMENT-REVIEW airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.19 expectation 2028-10-07 High-materiality use cases need formal independent validation by competent, objective personnel independent of development and deployment, covering conceptual soundness, data, implementation integrity, evaluation results, explainability/fairness, assumptions. AIRM-5.19-INDEPENDENT-VALIDATION airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.20 expectation 2028-10-07 Non-high-materiality use cases may use other documented reviews, such as peer review by qualified individuals not involved in development or deployment. AIRM-5.18-PRE-DEPLOYMENT-REVIEW airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.21 expectation 2028-10-07 Reviewers report findings, limitations, remediation and conditions of use to the approval body, which ensures recommendations are actioned. AIRM-5.21-FINDINGS-ACTIONED airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.22 expectation 2028-10-07 Technology and cybersecurity reviews before production: secure design, least privilege, deployment checklists confirming encryption, DLP, firewalls, access, logging; vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, red teaming and adversarial testing with safeguards. AIRM-5.22-SECURITY-REVIEW airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.23 expectation 2028-10-07 Ongoing monitoring of all deployed AI proportionate to materiality: metrics and tiered thresholds, drift checks, agent reasoning/action/tool monitoring, incident management with kill switches for high risk, accountable roles, records and access logging, training. AIRM-5.3-KILL-SWITCH, AIRM-5.23-MONITORING-MEASURES, AIRM-5.23-AGENT-TRACE-MONITORING, AIRM-5.23-GENAI-LOGGING, AIRM-5.23-INCIDENT-MANAGEMENT, AIRM-5.23-ACCOUNTABLE-PERSON, AIRM-5.23-TRAINING-AWARENESS airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.24 expectation 2028-10-07 Re-validate or review AI as needed, with frequency and rigour informed by materiality; high-materiality use cases get regular independent re-validation; triggers include interconnected findings, monitoring breaches, significant changes, new external risks. AIRM-5.24-REVALIDATION airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.25 expectation 2028-10-07 Comprehensive change controls: a framework to grade change significance with review and re-approval for significant changes (compensating monitoring where prior review is impossible); change control with version tracking and rollback; enhanced controls for automatic updates. AIRM-5.11-CHANGE-NOTIFICATION, AIRM-5.25-CHANGE-FRAMEWORK, AIRM-5.25-CHANGE-CONTROL, AIRM-5.25-DYNAMIC-UPDATES airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §5.26 expectation 2028-10-07 Controls for retirement or decommissioning when AI is no longer needed or exceeds risk tolerance: dependencies, data retention, secure removal from production, stakeholder notification. AIRM-5.26-RETIREMENT airm.controls, airm.evals, airm.monitor, airm.thirdparty §6.1 expectation 2028-10-07 Ensure competence and proper conduct of personnel developing, deploying and using AI: recruit talent, train, build culture; allocate human, technological and financial resources proportionate to risk. AIRM-5.23-TRAINING-AWARENESS, AIRM-6.1-COMPETENCE airm.controls §6.2 expectation 2028-10-07 Regularly review that personnel have adequate capability and capacity, and that training programmes stay current for newer AI technologies. AIRM-5.23-TRAINING-AWARENESS, AIRM-6.1-COMPETENCE airm.controls §6.3 expectation 2028-10-07 Technology infrastructure (compute, network, memory, secure data pipelines) must meet performance, scalability and resilience needs, considering technology risk management guidelines and industry frameworks. AIRM-6.3-INFRASTRUCTURE airm.controls

docs.title: Footnotes that carry requirements
docs.text:
Several footnotes carry expectations rather than references, and the toolkit treats them as binding.

Footnote Anchored to Kind Summary fn1 §1.1 definition FI as defined in Section 2 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022. fn4 §1.2 scope Consolidated supervision covers locally incorporated banking and insurance FIs. fn5 §1.2 definition Critical information infrastructure as defined in the Cybersecurity Act 2018. fn6 §1.3 scope In-scope examples: machine learning, deep learning, NLP, computer vision, generative AI/LLMs, AI agents and multi-agent systems. Out of scope: rule-based systems, manually specified formulae, fixed RPA. fn7 §1.4 definition Use case / system / model are used explicitly where a point is specific to one. fn10 §1.10 definition Third-party AI: AI systems or models, and services or tools incorporating AI, developed, owned, operated or provided externally that an FI procures, subscribes to, accesses or relies on. fn13 §2.4 expectation Humans in the 2.4 example use cases should review and check outputs before use. fn20 §3.5 definition AI incident means an incident involving failure, malfunction or poor performance of the underlying AI system(s) or model(s). fn21 §4.2 scope Embedded AI example: SaaS not sold as AI but containing AI features the FI uses. fn22 §4.4 guidance Shadow-AI mitigations: staff guidance on allowed/disallowed uses including embedded features and public tools, and technical controls such as network monitoring and data loss prevention to detect unauthorised AI use. fn23 §4.6 guidance Linkages via consistent data asset identifiers to data inventories and vendor/service identifiers to third-party registers. fn24 §4.7 expectation Differences in attributes captured across use cases must be delineated in policy; omissions must not compromise oversight. fn25 §4.8 guidance Agent inventory attributes: agent-specific identifiers, tools and systems the agent can access, its components, and the guardrails imposed. fn26 §4.10 expectation Dependencies between AI systems or models supporting a use case should be considered where they affect its risk profile. fn27 §5.1 definition AI life cycle spans inception to retirement (adapted from ISO/IEC 22989). fn28 §5.2 expectation Partial deployments (pilots, phased rollouts) need policies governing deviations from standard controls: time and user limits, success criteria, terms of use, close monitoring, scope compliance. fn29 §5.3 definition Kill switches are mechanisms to deactivate AI expeditiously if it exceeds risk tolerances. fn32 §5.5 definition Transparency is disclosure to affected individuals plus explanations on request; explainability is methods (built-in or post-hoc) for understanding outputs. fn34 §5.6 guidance Customer disclosures need not be technical (effects, basis for decisions, redress); technical detail suits internal evaluators; IMDA chatbot transparency guidelines referenced. fn36 §5.8 expectation Proxies for, or attributes highly correlated with, protected attributes must also be considered. fn37 §5.9 scope Human oversight expectations cover every case where the FI judged human involvement necessary, whether in-the-loop or over-the-loop. fn38 §5.10 scope Development controls apply where the FI modifies or fine-tunes third-party AI before deployment. fn39 §5.10 scope MAS outsourcing and third-party service expectations apply to third-party AI. fn41 §5.12 definition Models include specific ML/DL models or techniques such as optimisation or fine-tuning. fn42 §5.12 definition Features are dataset attributes; feature engineering creates or transforms them. fn45 §5.15 guidance Pilots or phased rollouts with guardrails can be used to obtain representative data when testing data is limited. fn46 §5.15 expectation GenAI testing must pay particular attention to hallucination, toxic/harmful/biased content, bias, data leakage or disclosure, and vulnerability to adversarial attack. fn48 §5.20 scope Reviewers must be independent of both initial and ongoing deployment (operation) of the AI. fn49 §5.25 guidance Change examples: training data, model/system architecture, key assumptions, scope of use, downstream impact.
