docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
airm version | init | scan | assess | check | evidence | report | gap | crosswalk | clauses | schemas

Every command prints the paragraph behind what it says, and ends with the standing disclaimer. Run airm <command> --help for the authoritative option list; this page explains when to reach for each one.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Nothing adverse found 1 At least one automated control check failed (§5.2 proportionate controls not met) 2 Usage or input error

needs_attestation does not fail the build. By construction it is a question for a person, and a pipeline that failed on it would teach people to suppress it.

docs.title: airm init
docs.text:
Scaffold a register, and optionally an editable copy of the rubric.

airm init --institution "Merlion Commercial Bank" --out ai-inventory.yaml --rubric-out rubric.yaml

-i/--institution, -o/--out, --rubric-out, --force.

docs.title: airm scan
docs.text:
Shadow-AI discovery over a directory: LLM SDK imports, model endpoints, MCP server configs, agent frameworks and vendor AI SaaS references (§4.2 fn21, §4.4 fn22). Emits candidate inventory entries for triage.

airm scan . --out candidates.yaml --min-confidence high --json scan.json

-o/--out, --json, --min-confidence (low|medium|high), --group-by (directory|file), --show.

Scan output is untrusted data

Findings come from files the toolkit did not write. They are never executed, imported or treated as configuration; secrets are redacted and symlinks are skipped. Triage candidates before merging them into a register.

docs.title: airm assess
docs.text:
Score Impact, Complexity and Reliance and derive the inherent and residual tiers (§4.10-§4.13).

airm assess -r ai-inventory.yaml --explain          # every score with its reasons
airm assess -r ai-inventory.yaml --write            # write ratings back into the register (§4.7)
airm assess -r ai-inventory.yaml -u kyc-document-agent --json assessment.json

-r/--register, --rubric, -u/--use-case, --explain, --write, --json.

docs.title: airm check
docs.text:
Evaluate the applicable controls for one use case, the whole register, or the institution-level controls (§5.2-§5.26, §3.3-§3.5). This is the command to put in CI.

airm check -r ai-inventory.yaml --trail evidence/trail.jsonl
airm check -r ai-inventory.yaml --institution
airm check -r ai-inventory.yaml -u kyc-document-agent --all --json results.json

-r/--register, -u/--use-case, --rubric, --controls, --trail, --institution, --all, --json.

docs.title: airm evidence
docs.text:
Append a record to the hash-chained trail, or verify it (§5.23(d), §5.17). Each --item is hashed, so a file changed after attestation is detectable.

airm evidence review -u kyc-document-agent -a "model.risk@bank" \
  --item "validation-report=evidence/kyc/validation.md" --outcome pass
airm evidence --verify -t evidence/trail.jsonl

-t/--trail, -u/--use-case, -a/--actor, --item (repeatable, name=path), --outcome, --severity, --verify.

docs.title: airm report
docs.text:
Generate the audit-ready pack: board one-pager, inventory register, materiality report, control applicability statement, gap analysis by effective date, crosswalk coverage, clause index, third-party assessments and summary.json.

airm report -r examples/synthetic_bank/ai-inventory.yaml \
  --vendors examples/synthetic_bank/third-party-assessments.yaml \
  --trail examples/synthetic_bank/evidence/trail.jsonl \
  -o audit-pack/ --docx

-r/--register, -o/--out, --rubric, --controls, --vendors, --trail, --docx.

docs.title: airm gap
docs.text:
Open items grouped by when the underlying clause takes effect (§1.8) — the view for a programme plan: what must be true by 7 October 2027, and what by 7 October 2028.

airm gap -r ai-inventory.yaml --by-date

docs.title: airm crosswalk
docs.text:
Query the mapping to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and its GenAI Profile, the EU AI Act, MAS FEAT and the MAS Information Paper (2024).

airm crosswalk -c 5.19                                  # what other frameworks say about §5.19
airm crosswalk -f iso_42001                             # everything ISO 42001 maps to
airm crosswalk --ref "Article 14"                        # reverse lookup
airm crosswalk --holding iso_42001,nist_ai_rmf           # residual work if you already hold these

-f/--framework, -c/--clause, --ref, --holding, --json.

docs.title: airm clauses
docs.text:
The clause index: every paragraph, its effective date, and the controls and module implementing it. Generated from the catalogue, so it cannot drift.

airm clauses --section 5 --tag agent --expectations
airm clauses --format markdown -o docs/clause-index.md

-s/--section, -t/--tag, --expectations, --format (table|markdown), -o/--out.

docs.title: airm schemas
docs.text:
Export a JSON Schema for every format the toolkit reads or writes, so a GRC platform, a spreadsheet or a service in another language can validate the same files.

airm schemas --out schemas

docs.title: airm version
docs.text: Prints the package version and the Guidelines edition the catalogue indexes, with its issue date and source hash.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The toolkit is built around five objects, in the order the Guidelines ask for them. Each one exists because a paragraph of the text requires it, and each carries the paragraph that does.

docs.title: 1. The clause catalogue — airm.catalog
docs.text:
Every paragraph of the Guidelines as data: identifier, section, heading, a summary of at most forty words in the authors' own words, a kind (expectation, definition, scope, context or guidance), who it applies to, its effective date under §1.8, and tags such as genai, agent, third-party, inventory, materiality and human-oversight. Footnotes are included where they carry a requirement: fn25 (agent inventory attributes), fn22 (controls for unidentified AI), fn46 (generative-AI failure modes) and 26 others.

from airm.catalog import load_catalogue

catalogue = load_catalogue()
print(len(catalogue), "paragraphs;", len(catalogue.expectations()), "expectations")
print(catalogue["5.15"].summary, catalogue["5.15"].effective)

Nothing else in the toolkit may cite a paragraph the catalogue does not contain; a test enforces it. That rule is the only mechanical defence against a control catalogue that drifts into invention, and it is why every citation in the paper can be traced to a line of YAML and from there to a page of the primary PDF.

docs.title: 2. The inventory — airm.inventory
docs.text:
A Register of UseCase entries carrying the attributes of §4.7 and fn24. A tool-using use case adds an AgentExtension with the fn25 attributes: agent identifier, approved tools, systems accessible, permissions, components, guardrails, human checkpoints, a step limit, whether the agent can initiate external actions, and whether its traces are logged.

Two behaviours are easy to trip over:

  • Autonomy and agency are validated together. An agentic autonomy level without an AgentExtension is a validation error, and so is the reverse. Build the object in one call; the two fields cannot be mutated in sequence.
  • airm scan produces candidates, not entries. Shadow-AI discovery (§4.4, fn22) is a heuristic over imports, endpoints, MCP configurations and SaaS references. Its output is data to be triaged, never configuration to be trusted, and a clean scan means the scanner found nothing, which is not the same as there being nothing.

docs.title: 3. Materiality — airm.materiality
docs.text:
A YAML rubric scores Impact, Complexity and Reliance (§4.12(a)–(c)) from 23 signals, each citing the paragraph it derives from, and combines them into an inherent tier — Low, Medium, High or Critical — and a residual tier after declared mitigations. Every score carries its reasons, so an assessment can be argued with rather than only accepted.

The rubric is a proposal

MAS prescribes no materiality methodology (Response to Feedback §7.19). The default rubric is the authors'. Fork it with airm init --rubric-out rubric.yaml and airm assess --rubric rubric.yaml.

Two default behaviours are worth knowing before you fork:

  • The impact gate. The tier is the highest of the three dimensions, but Complexity and Reliance may raise it at most one level above Impact. The gate implements Response §7.9 (Complexity is not a standalone driver) and §7.5 (anchor on the consequences of failure), and it is why an internal research assistant does not become Critical for using an LLM.
  • No generative-AI use case can be rated Low. GenAI sets Complexity to High, and the gate then permits one level above Impact. This is a consequence of the defaults, reported in the paper as a finding rather than tuned away.

docs.title: 4. Controls and outcomes — airm.controls
docs.text:
Each control carries its clause references, applicability by inherent tier and by scope, the evidence items it requires, an optional automated check, and an automatability class:

Class Meaning Best possible outcome auto A deterministic function of the entry and its evidence decides the outcome PASS semi The artefact's presence and currency are checkable; its adequacy is not NEEDS_ATTESTATION doc Organisational or judgemental; there is no artefact to inspect NEEDS_ATTESTATION

A semi control never reports PASS

When a semi control's automated check succeeds, the outcome is NEEDS_ATTESTATION: the toolkit found the artefact and confirmed it is current, and a person must judge whether it is adequate. Read the attestation count as a work queue, not a failure count. airm check exits non-zero only on a genuine FAIL, because a pipeline that failed on attestations would teach people to suppress them.

Scope matters too. Most controls are evaluated per use case; seven are evaluated once per institution — the §3.3–§3.5 control functions and the §4.1–§4.4 identification process. The paper's RQ1 measures how the classes are distributed across the Guidelines: 84.6% of Section 4 expectations are auto, none of Section 3's are.

docs.title: 5. Evidence — airm.monitor
docs.text:
An append-only JSONL trail in which each record carries the hash of the previous one and a digest of every evidence file it points at. airm evidence --verify detects both a broken chain and a file that changed after it was attested, which is what §5.23(d) and §5.17 need an auditor to be able to do: confirm that the evidence on the table is the evidence that was signed off.

Incidents have their own schema, following the fn20 definition in §5.23(b).

docs.title: How they compose
docs.text:
airm scan      →  candidate entries           (§4.2, §4.4)
airm init      →  register + rubric
airm assess    →  tiers, with reasons         (§4.10–§4.13)
airm check     →  outcomes, with evidence     (§5.2–§5.26)
airm evidence  →  hash-chained trail          (§5.23(d))
airm report    →  the audit pack              (§3.4, §4.5, §5.2, §1.8)
airm gap       →  what is missing, by effective date
airm crosswalk →  what ISO / NIST / EU already cover
airm schemas   →  every format as JSON Schema

The cookbook walks through each of these with a snippet that was run against the shipped example.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Recipes in the order a team usually needs them. Every snippet runs against the shipped worked example, so you can try it before touching your own register.

docs.title: Gate CI on control failures
docs.text:
airm check exits 1 on a genuine automated failure and 0 when the only open items are attestations, so it can gate a pipeline without punishing teams for work that is a human's to do.

# .github/workflows/ai-governance.yml
- run: pip install airmkit
- run: airm check --register ai-inventory.yaml --trail evidence/trail.jsonl
- run: airm check --register ai-inventory.yaml --institution

Add --json results.json and upload it as an artefact if you want the outcomes in your GRC tool.

docs.title: See why a use case is rated the way it is
docs.text:
airm assess -r examples/synthetic_bank/ai-inventory.yaml -u kyc-document-agent --explain

Every dimension prints the signals that fired and the paragraph each derives from. If you disagree with a signal, you are disagreeing with a line of YAML, which is the point.

docs.title: Fork the rubric
docs.text:
airm init --rubric-out rubric.yaml      # editable copy of the defaults
$EDITOR rubric.yaml                     # change weights, thresholds, the impact gate
airm assess -r ai-inventory.yaml --rubric rubric.yaml

Keep the clause field on every signal you add. A signal with no paragraph behind it is a house view, not a MAS expectation, and the gap analysis will treat it as one.

docs.title: Find AI nobody declared
docs.text:
airm scan . --min-confidence high --out candidates.yaml

Then triage candidates.yaml by hand into the register. §4.4 and fn22 ask for the residual risk from unidentified AI to be managed, so record the decision as well as the findings:

airm evidence shadow-ai-sweep -a "model.risk@bank" \
  --item "scan-report=evidence/scan-2027-01.json" --outcome pass

docs.title: Audit an agent's tool use against its approved scope
docs.text:
Serves §5.23(a) with fn25: did the agent only use the tools its inventory entry approves?

from airm.evals import tool_scope_audit
from airm.inventory import Register

register = Register.load("examples/synthetic_bank/ai-inventory.yaml")
use_case = register.get("kyc-document-agent")

observed = ["ocr_extract", "registry_lookup", "email_send"]   # names pulled from your traces
audit = tool_scope_audit(use_case, observed, calls=412)

print(audit.unapproved)   # ['email_send'] — used but outside the approved scope
print(audit.unused)       # approved but never used: scope to tighten
print(audit.clauses)      # the paragraphs this audit serves

Tool names from traces are compared as strings and never resolved or invoked.

docs.title: Map an eval harness result to a control
docs.text:
The toolkit does not run evaluations; it reads what your harness already produced and maps it to the control that needs it (§5.14-§5.15).

from airm.evals import from_inspect, from_garak, from_ragas

robustness = from_garak("garak-report.jsonl", use_case_id="customer-service-chatbot")
faithfulness = from_ragas("ragas.json", use_case_id="policy-rag-assistant")

print(robustness.failure_modes_covered)   # mapped to the fn46 failure modes
print(faithfulness.passed)                # against the thresholds you pass in
print(faithfulness.model, faithfulness.model_digest, faithfulness.seed)  # recorded for §5.17

Adapters exist for inspect-ai, promptfoo, garak, ragas and deepeval. Store the result as an evidence record so the control check can find it.

docs.title: Measure guardrail effectiveness, honestly
docs.text:
§5.15 fn46 asks for guardrail effectiveness to be tested. The probe runner ships 20 probes across jailbreak, indirect injection, PII leakage and policy evasion — plus a benign in-scope control set, because a guardrail that refuses everything scores perfectly on attacks.

from airm.evals.probes import GuardrailPattern, MockBackend, run_suite

result = run_suite(MockBackend(), patterns=[GuardrailPattern.FILTER, GuardrailPattern.LAYERED])
for run in result.runs:
    rate, successes, trials = run.asr()
    refusal, refusals, benign = run.over_refusal()
    print(run.pattern, f"ASR {rate:.1%} ({successes}/{trials})",
          f"over-refusal {refusal:.1%} ({refusals}/{benign})",
          "meets High tier:", run.meets_tier("High"))

meets_tier tests the upper Wilson bound against the proposed per-tier limit, so a small sample cannot manufacture a pass: 0 successes in 16 trials still fails the High tier. Swap MockBackend() for OllamaBackend("qwen3.5:0.8b") to measure a real local model. Read the OllamaBackend docstring first: it documents two measurement defects we hit, including an empty-completion bug that produced a false 0% attack success rate.

docs.title: Verify evidence has not changed
docs.text:
airm evidence --verify -t examples/synthetic_bank/evidence/trail.jsonl

Reports a broken hash chain and any evidence file whose digest no longer matches what was attested.

docs.title: Answer "we already hold ISO 42001 — what is left?"
docs.text:
airm crosswalk --holding iso_42001,nist_ai_rmf

Prints the expectations with no full mapping. On our crosswalk that residue is governance machinery and MAS-specific proportionality, not the agent clauses.

docs.title: Produce the audit pack
docs.text:
airm report -r examples/synthetic_bank/ai-inventory.yaml \
  --vendors examples/synthetic_bank/third-party-assessments.yaml \
  --trail examples/synthetic_bank/evidence/trail.jsonl \
  -o audit-pack/ --docx

Nine documents, starting with 00-board-summary.md. The pack also writes summary.json, which is the machine-readable version of every count in it.

docs.title: Validate files without Python
docs.text:
check-jsonschema --schemafile schemas/ai-inventory-register.schema.json ai-inventory.yaml

All 20 formats are exported as JSON Schema; regenerate with airm schemas.

docs.title: Reproduce the study
docs.text:
make quick        # lint, fast tests, worked example — under 5 minutes
make reproduce    # every table and figure in the paper, no hosted API

make reproduce ends by printing a git diff --stat of results/, schemas/, paper/ and docs/. An empty diff means your clone reproduces the published run.

docs.title: Literature review
docs.text: Scope: the regulatory and academic material that an implementer of the MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management (MAS-AIRM, 7 Oct 2026) needs in order to turn the text into controls, and the evidence base for the five research questions in docs/RESEARCH_QUESTIONS.md. Citation keys refer to refs.bib. Where a claim rests on a document we could not download as a primary source it is marked [UNVERIFIED].

docs.title: 1. MAS primary documents
docs.text:
MAS-AIRM (2026) [@mas2026airm] is a principles-based, 30-page document with 65 numbered paragraphs and 51 footnotes. Fifty-one paragraphs are expectations ("should"), the rest scope, definitions and context (see src/airm/catalog/mas_airm_2026.yaml). It is deliberately non-prescriptive about metrics, thresholds and the aggregation of its three materiality dimensions (Response §7.19, §10.28). Its distinctive features relative to earlier MAS material are (i) a use-case-anchored risk materiality assessment with Impact / Complexity / Reliance (§4.12), (ii) an inventory expectation with named attributes (§4.7) extended to agents (fn25), (iii) explicit treatment of shadow AI and embedded AI (§4.2, §4.4), (iv) guardrail-effectiveness testing for GenAI and agents (§5.15), and (v) third-party AI accountability with a limit / suspend / replace expectation (§5.11).

Response to Feedback (2026) [@mas2026response] is the authoritative gloss. It settles several points that the Guidelines leave open: high-risk triggers key on inherent materiality (§7.21); evaluation is at use-case level (§10.30); vendor self-attestations are not acceptable substitutes for transparency (§9.9); contingency plans are required only for high-risk use cases (§10.70); no AI-specific incident reporting regime is introduced (§10.69). docs/WHAT_CHANGED.md lists 36 changes.

Consultation paper P017-2025 (2025) [@mas2025consult] contained the draft text plus an Annex with a workflow-dependence applicability test that was dropped in the final version.

Information Paper on AI Model Risk Management (Dec 2024) [@mas2024infopaper] reports good practices from a thematic review of banks. Its chapter structure (governance; identification, inventory, materiality; development, validation, deployment, monitoring, change; GenAI; third-party AI) is the template the Guidelines follow, and it supplies the concrete practices (e.g., materiality tiers used by banks, validation scopes) that the Guidelines abstract away. The toolkit's default rubric levels borrow from the Info Paper's observed practice rather than from the Guidelines, which name dimensions but not levels.

FEAT Principles (2018) [@mas2018feat] remain in force (§1.2) and are the named reference for "fair" outcomes (fn35). The 14 principles are organised as Fairness (justifiability; accuracy and bias), Ethics, Accountability (internal; external) and Transparency. They are the source of the crosswalk's FEAT column.

Veritas (2021–2023) [@mas2022veritas3; @mas2022veritas3a; @mas2022veritas3c; @mas2023veritas5] provides assessment methodologies and an open-source fairness toolkit (veritastool, Apache-2.0) for tabular models. Veritas Document 3A's fairness methodology (define fairness objectives → choose metric → measure → mitigate → document) is the pattern airm.evals.fairness follows; Document 3C's transparency questions inform the transparency control's evidence list. Veritas pre-dates LLMs and has no guidance on generative or agentic systems.

docs.title: 2. International frameworks used in the crosswalk
docs.text:
NIST AI RMF 1.0 (2023) [@nist2023airmf] organises practice into Govern, Map, Measure, Manage with 72 subcategories. MAS-AIRM footnotes 31 and 51 cite it directly. The Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, 2024) [@nist2024genai] adds 12 GenAI risk categories (e.g., confabulation, information security, value-chain and component integration) and ~200 suggested actions, which is the most granular public source for GenAI controls and maps well onto MAS-AIRM §5.15/fn46.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 [@iso2023_42001] is a certifiable AI management-system standard. Its Annex A controls (A.2–A.10) cover policy, roles, resources, impact assessment, lifecycle, data, information for interested parties, use, and third-party relationships. The Response (§9.7–9.9) explicitly contemplates ISO 42001 certification of vendors as evidence. ISO/IEC 23894:2023 [@iso2023_23894] (AI risk management guidance) and ISO/IEC 22989:2022 [@iso2022_22989] (terminology; cited in MAS-AIRM fn27) supply vocabulary.

EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) [@eu2024aiact] imposes obligations on providers and deployers of high-risk systems (Arts. 9 risk management, 10 data governance, 11–12 documentation and logging, 13 transparency, 14 human oversight, 15 accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, 17 QMS, 26 deployer obligations, 72 post-market monitoring). Credit scoring and life/health insurance pricing are listed high-risk uses (Annex III §5), so the overlap with MAS-AIRM §5.6–5.8 is substantial. The Act is binding law with conformity assessment; MAS-AIRM is supervisory guidance.

docs.title: 3. Comparable financial-sector guidance
docs.text:
• US Fed SR 11-7 / OCC 2011-12 [@fed2011sr117] is the ancestor of all "model risk management" (MRM) text: model inventory, validation (conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, outcomes analysis), independence and effective challenge, governance. MAS-AIRM §5.17–5.19 and §5.24 are recognisably SR 11-7 concepts restated for AI.
  • Bank of England PRA SS1/23 (2023) [@pra2023ss123] sets five principles (model identification and classification; governance; development, implementation and use; independent validation; model risk mitigants) with a model tiering requirement that parallels MAS-AIRM §4.10–4.13.
  • HKMA has issued principles on consumer protection in the use of GenAI (2024) [@hkma2024genai] and a circular on the use of AI in monitoring suspicious activities; BNM (Malaysia) consulted on AI risk management for financial institutions in 2025 [UNVERIFIED: text not acquired]. These are the natural next crosswalk targets (CONTRIBUTING.md).
  • BIS FSI Insights No. 63 (2024) [@bis2024fsi63] surveys AI regulation across jurisdictions and identifies inventories, materiality tiering and third-party dependency as the common supervisory building blocks.
  • FSB (2024) [@fsb2024ai] highlights third-party dependency and concentration as the financial-stability channel, which MAS-AIRM §1.10(d), §5.11(c) and fn18 echo.

docs.title: 4.1 Agent governance and visibility (§1.11, fn25, §5.9, §5.23(a))
docs.text: Chan et al. [@chan2023harms] taxonomise harms from increasingly agentic systems; Chan et al. [@chan2024visibility] argue for agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logs as visibility measures, which is almost exactly fn25 + §5.23(a)(d). Shavit et al. [@shavit2023agentic] (OpenAI) propose practices for governing agentic systems including scoped permissions, default behaviours and attributability. Kapoor et al. [@kapoor2024agents] show agent benchmarks conflate accuracy with cost and lack holdout sets, cautioning against naive use of benchmark scores as "evaluation measures" under §5.14(a). Ruan et al. [@ruan2024toolemu] (ToolEmu) and Debenedetti et al. [@debenedetti2024agentdojo] (AgentDojo) provide sandboxed environments for measuring unsafe tool use and indirect prompt injection in agents; Zhan et al. [@zhan2024injecagent] benchmark indirect injection specifically against tool-integrated agents.

docs.title: 4.2 Guardrail evaluation and adversarial robustness (§5.15, fn46, §5.22(b))
docs.text: Greshake et al. [@greshake2023indirect] introduced indirect prompt injection; Perez & Ribeiro [@perez2022ignore] direct injection; Wei et al. [@wei2023jailbroken] explain jailbreaks as competing objectives and mismatched generalisation; Zou et al. [@zou2023gcg] show transferable adversarial suffixes; Chao et al. [@chao2023pair] automate jailbreaks with an attacker LLM. HarmBench [@mazeika2024harmbench] standardises red-team evaluation. On the defence side, Llama Guard [@inan2023llamaguard] and NeMo Guardrails [@rebedea2023nemo] are the canonical classifier- and rail-based guardrail patterns; garak [@derczynski2024garak] is the open-source LLM vulnerability scanner the toolkit adapts. OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications [@owasp2025llm] and MITRE ATLAS [@mitre2024atlas] give the threat vocabulary used in airm.controls security controls.

docs.title: 4.3 LLM evaluation validity (§5.14, §5.17)
docs.text: HELM [@liang2022helm] established multi-metric, scenario-based evaluation; Zheng et al. [@zheng2023judge] quantify LLM-as-judge agreement with humans (~80 %) and its biases (position, verbosity, self-enhancement), which matters when §5.14(a) thresholds are computed by a judge model. RAGAS [@es2023ragas] and FActScore [@min2023factscore] operationalise faithfulness and factual precision for RAG; Ji et al. [@ji2023hallucination] survey hallucination. Inspect [@aisi2024inspect] (UK AI Security Institute) is the eval harness whose log format the toolkit reads. Weidinger et al. [@weidinger2022taxonomy] give the risk taxonomy that NIST AI 600-1 and fn46 compress.

docs.title: 4.4 Documentation, auditability and accountability (§5.17, §5.21, §5.23(d))
docs.text: Model Cards [@mitchell2019modelcards] and Datasheets [@gebru2021datasheets] are the de-facto templates for §5.17(a)–(f); Raji et al. [@raji2020audit] define the internal audit framework (scoping, mapping, artefact collection, testing, reflection) that §5.18–5.21 presuppose.

docs.title: 4.5 Fairness (§5.7–5.8)
docs.text: Hardt et al. [@hardt2016equality] (equalised odds / equal opportunity) and the Barocas–Hardt–Narayanan text [@barocas2023fairml] cover the metric landscape; Veritas 3A chooses among them for credit and insurance. fn36's proxy requirement is the "proxy discrimination" problem these sources formalise.

docs.title: 4.6 Model risk management for ML
docs.text: The SR 11-7 lineage is reinterpreted for ML in the Info Paper [@mas2024infopaper] and PRA SS1/23 [@pra2023ss123]; the academic MRM literature is thin and mostly practitioner-authored. Bommasani et al. [@bommasani2021foundation] frame the foundation-model supply chain that makes §5.11(b)–(c) (supply chain, concentration) necessary.

docs.title: 5. Gap table: MAS expectations without an established implementation pattern
docs.text:
MAS-AIRM clause Expectation Established pattern? Closest available Gap §4.4, fn22 Keep residual risk from unidentified AI within appetite No DLP/CASB logs; SBOM-style scanning No standard for measuring shadow-AI coverage; airm scan is a repo-level heuristic only §4.2, fn21 Identify embedded AI in material third-party services No Vendor questionnaires; AI BOM proposals No machine-readable vendor AI disclosure format §4.12 Combine Impact / Complexity / Reliance into a tier Partial PRA SS1/23 tiering; bank practice in Info Paper No public rubric; this toolkit proposes one (RQ2) fn25 Agent attributes: tools/systems accessible, guardrails Partial Chan et al. 2024 visibility; MCP/tool manifests No inventory schema standard; proposed in schemas/ §5.15, fn46 Test effectiveness of guardrails Partial HarmBench, garak, AgentDojo No accepted threshold per risk tier (RQ3) §5.23(a) Monitor agent reasoning, actions, tools Partial OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions; tracing No link from traces to approved scope checks; toolkit adds tool-scope audit §5.23(d) Prompt/response logging with model version and reasoning Partial Tracing frameworks Retention, privacy and tamper-evidence not standardised; toolkit uses hash-chained JSONL §5.25(a),(c) Significance of changes incl. prompt/model-version changes and auto-updates No Software change management No agreed taxonomy of "significant" LLM changes; toolkit records both §5.3 Tested kill-switch protocols for high-risk AI No BCP/DR testing No evidence format for "kill switch tested"; toolkit treats as attestation §5.9 Automation bias and decision fatigue No HCI literature No operational metric; attestation only §6.1–6.2 Competence of AI users No Training completion records Attestation only

The gap table drives RQ1 (which clauses can be automated) and docs/FUTURE_WORK.md.

docs.title: LinkedIn drafts
docs.text:
One draft per Guidelines section, plus a launch post and a "what we learned" post. Each is at most 1,300 characters, carries one concrete finding or artefact, and ends with the repository link.

The drafts were written by Claude Fable 5.1 from the result files. The .md.in files are the sources; the .md files are generated by experiments/render_paper.py (make paper) with every number injected from results/summary.json. Edit the template, never the output: a hand-edited draft would drift from the paper the first time an experiment is re-run. A test enforces the character limit, the trailing link and the absence of unresolved placeholders.

# Draft Clauses Finding it carries 01 01-launch.md — What the toolkit is; the automatability headline 02 02-applicability.md §2.2-§2.5 The applicability test changed from "integrated use" to material adverse impact 03 03-governance.md §3.3-§3.6 Section 3 is 0% automatable, and why that is correct 04 04-inventory.md §4.2-§4.9, fn21, fn22, fn25 An inventory must account for what is not in it 05 05-materiality.md §4.10-§4.13 Autonomy moves the control set, not the tier; no GenAI use case can be Low 06 06-lifecycle.md §5.1-§5.26 A semi control never reports PASS; attestation is not failure 07 07-guardrails.md §5.15, fn46 The patterns that suppress attacks refuse half of benign in-scope traffic 08 08-third-party.md §5.10-§5.11 Third-party AI tightened; an ISO 42001 certificate does not test model behaviour 09 09-crosswalk.md all The ISO+NIST+EU residue is governance, not the agent clauses 10 10-what-we-learned.md — The refutations, and the measurement bug that produced a perfect score

docs.title: 01 launch
docs.text:
The MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management bind from 7 October 2027. We built an open-source toolkit that turns them into machine-checkable controls, then measured how far that actually works.

In the box: - A machine-readable catalogue: 65 paragraphs, 51 expectations, 29 footnotes that carry requirements (the fn25 agent attributes among them). - 65 controls, each citing the paragraph it serves and labelled by how far it can be automated. - A 224-row crosswalk to ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF and its GenAI Profile, the EU AI Act, FEAT and the 2024 MAS Information Paper. - A worked example on a fictional bank with 8 synthetic use cases, and five pre-registered experiments.

The headline: 45.1% of expectations admit a fully automated check. Section 4 (inventory, materiality) is 84.6% automatable; Section 3 (governance) is 0.0%.

Of 17 hypotheses fixed before the experiments ran, 7 were refuted. All of them are in the paper, with the thresholds they failed.

Read it: https://thanatchon36.github.io/airmkit/paper/

Not affiliated with MAS. Not legal advice. Apache-2.0.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 02 applicability
docs.text:
Section 2 of the MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines is the clause most firms will misread, because it changed late and quietly.

The November 2025 draft asked whether AI was "an integrated part of business processes", with an annex flowchart and a list of examples. The final text deletes both and asks instead whether your AI use could have a material adverse impact (§2.2-§2.4). Below that line, a basic governance regime applies (§2.5); above it, everything.

That is easier to satisfy and harder to evidence. "Integrated into a process" is a fact about architecture. "Material adverse impact" is a judgement you must record, defend and periodically re-check - §2.5(f) adds that last duty explicitly.

We tracked 36 substantive changes from draft to final with a paragraph concordance. §2.2 is also the one expectation in our catalogue with no implementing control: it is the roll-up clause that says Sections 3-6 apply, so a control for it would always pass. We report it as uncovered rather than write a control that cannot fail.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 03 governance
docs.text:
We classified every expectation in the MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines by how far a machine can check it. Section 3 - governance and oversight - scored 0.0% automatable.

That is not a tooling gap; it is what the section is. §3.4 asks the board to approve and regularly review the strategic direction for AI use. §3.6 asks local senior management to be able to demonstrate oversight to MAS even under a group framework. No artefact a program can inspect settles either without reducing it to a signature.

What a tool can do is narrower and still worth having: hold the named control functions for identification, inventory and materiality (§3.3-§3.5) as structured fields, check they are named and distinct, and generate the board one-pager from the register rather than retyping it.

Section 4, by contrast, is 84.6% automatable. Governance does not automate; the register does. Plan the effort accordingly, and treat any vendor claiming to automate Section 3 with suspicion.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 04 inventory
docs.text:
The MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines ask an inventory a question most inventories cannot answer: what is not in you?

§4.4 and fn22 require the residual risk from unidentified AI - shadow AI, embedded AI - to be kept within appetite, with mitigations. §4.2 and fn21 require identification to cover AI embedded in services from material third-party providers. Neither is satisfiable by a register filled from what teams declare.

fn25 then lists what an agentic entry needs: agent identifiers, the tools and systems it can access, its components, its guardrails. Most inventory schemas have nowhere to put them.

So the toolkit ships an inventory schema with an agent extension (also as JSON Schema, for GRC tools), plus airm scan, which walks a repository and flags LLM SDK imports, model endpoints, MCP server configs, agent frameworks and vendor AI SaaS as candidate entries. It is a heuristic, not coverage, and its output is data to triage, never configuration to trust.

Section 4 is the most automatable part of the Guidelines (84.6%) and the first to bind, on 7 Oct 2027. Start here.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 05 materiality
docs.text:
MAS will not give you a materiality formula. Response to Feedback §7.19 says a prescribed methodology would not suit every institution. §4.12 names three axes - Impact, Complexity, Reliance - and leaves the combination to you.

So we published one, to be argued with: 23 signals, each citing the paragraph it derives from, an inherent and a residual tier, every score carrying its reasons, all in editable YAML.

Two things it taught us:

An agent raises the control set, not the tier. Moving a use case up a six-rung autonomy ladder, 7 controls first bind at the agent step - guardrail testing, tool permissions, trace monitoring - but only 1 of 4 use cases changed tier. Tier is dominated by consequence. A review process keyed on tier will miss the agent step entirely.

Under our defaults, no generative-AI use case can be rated Low: GenAI sets Complexity to High and the impact gate permits one level above Impact. We report that as a finding rather than tune it away. If you think the gate is wrong, it is one line of YAML.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 06 lifecycle
docs.text:
One detail changes how you should read any AI control report, including ours.

In the Section 5 lifecycle clauses of the MAS Guidelines, most expectations are not "does the artefact exist" but "is the artefact adequate". So in our catalogue such a control is labelled semi: a machine confirms the artefact exists and is current; a human judges adequacy.

A semi control therefore never reports PASS. When its automated check succeeds, the outcome is NEEDS_ATTESTATION.

On the fictional portfolio that means 277 checks need attestation and 30 are genuine automated failures. Read the first number as failures and you will panic; read it as a work queue and it is the honest answer.

Counted per control, semi is the largest class (36.9%), ahead of auto (30.8%) and doc (32.3%). And 93.1% of estimated compliance effort sits in the semi and doc classes - the part no tool finishes for you.

Section 5 binds from 7 Oct 2028. The work is mostly people.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 07 guardrails
docs.text:
§5.15 and fn46 of the MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines require guardrails for generative AI and agents to be tested for effectiveness. We measured five common patterns on a local model against 20 probes - jailbreak, indirect injection, PII leakage, policy evasion - plus a benign in-scope control set.

Attack success: - no guardrail 75.0% - system prompt only 50.0% - deterministic filter 12.5% - LLM judge 12.5% - filter + judge 6.2%

Layering looks excellent. Then the benign set: over-refusal is 0.0% unguarded, 50.0% with the system prompt and 50.0% layered. The patterns that suppress attacks refuse half of ordinary requests.

Against our pre-registered joint criterion - attack success within the tier limit and over-refusal at or below 5.0% - 0 of 5 patterns qualified. The only pattern with a large reduction at zero over-refusal was the deterministic filter.

A guardrail report without a benign control set is unfalsifiable. Ask for one before you read the attack numbers.

One small local model, n=16 per pattern: a demonstration, not a general estimate.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 08 third party
docs.text:
The MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines got stricter on third-party AI between consultation and final text, while easing almost everywhere else.

§5.10-§5.11 state the institution's primary accountability for its use of third-party AI, require the ability to limit, suspend or replace a provider when residual risk exceeds appetite, and accept certifications or independent external assessments - while Response to Feedback §9.9 says a vendor self-attestation unsupported by evidence is generally not an effective way to close a transparency gap. Contractual visibility must cover AI introduction and updates, and development controls apply when you fine-tune (fn38).

So the toolkit models a vendor assessment over the eight §5.11 considerations, records whether assurance is independent or self-attested, tracks whether you tested the service yourself, and forces the residual-risk-versus-appetite decision to be written down with a limit/suspend/replace record.

One crosswalk result worth knowing: §5.11 has no full mapping in ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF or the EU AI Act. An ISO 42001 certificate shows a provider has a management system. It does not test the provider's model.

https://github.com/thanatchon36/airmkit

docs.title: 09 crosswalk
docs.text:
If you hold ISO/IEC 42001 and align to the NIST AI RMF, how much of the MAS AI Risk Management Guidelines is already done?

We hand-authored 224 mapping rows over 51 expectations, counting an unmapped expectation against coverage rather than excluding it.

  • ISO/IEC 42001: 37.2% fully covered
  • NIST AI RMF: 49.0%
  • EU AI Act: 43.1%
  • NIST GenAI Profile: 29.4% (narrow, accurate where it applies)
  • Union of ISO + NIST + EU AI Act: 64.7%, leaving 35.3% with no full mapping

We pre-registered the prediction that the residue would be the agent and generative-AI clauses. It was refuted. Those are covered. What no framework fully covers is governance machinery and Singapore-specific proportionality: the applicability test and basic regime (§2.2, §2.5), board responsibilities (§3.4), identification and shadow AI (§4.1, §4.4), materiality arbitration (§4.13), third-party accountability (§5.11), independent validation scope (§5.20).

Mapping is interpretive and asymmetric - a management-system standard, product law and voluntary guidance are not commensurable - so 18 rows are flagged low confidence and listed one by one.

We pre-registered 17 hypotheses before running the experiments behind our MAS AI Risk Management toolkit. 7 were refuted. The refutations were the useful part.

Automation flatters itself depending on the unit of analysis. At paragraph level 45.1% of expectations look automatable, because a paragraph takes the best class among its controls. Per control, the semi-automated class is largest. We report the pre-registered number and say which one we trust.

A measurement bug produced a perfect score. Our guardrail runner used a reasoning model; with thinking enabled the whole token budget went to the thinking channel and the content came back empty. An empty response matches no attack pattern, so every attack scored as "the guardrail held" - 0% attack success across five patterns, no error raised. Then five detectors proved mis-calibrated, one counting a refusal as a success. Both are disclosed in the result file and in the paper.

Proportionality scales rigour, not volume. Critical-tier use cases needed 91.4 evidence items on average against 92.0 at Medium. Same artefacts, deeper review.

If you publish only what held, you are not reporting. You are advertising.
